titre_video: The Solar Storm That Could Shut Down the AI Economy

segments.titre: Digital blackout and the lie behind AI data centers
segments.resume: Opening hook: the world faces a possible digital blackout. For over a century astrophysicists believed solar storms could only brew deep in the sun's core, so the data centers powering the AI revolution were built unprotected. Invisible plasma whirlpools have now been caught tearing the sun's outer crust, striking faster and harder than expected, and a single hit could collapse global infrastructure.
segments.texte: The world is staring down the barrel of a digital blackout. For over a century, astrophysicists thought solar storms could only brew deep in the sun’s core. Because of that, the multi-billion dollar data centers powering the AI revolution were built unprotected. They were built on a lie. Scientists have caught invisible plasma whirlpools tearing the sun’s outer crust. And they strike faster and harder than we thought. A single hit won’t cause a flicker of your lights. It will collapse our global infrastructure. And it’s already too late to stop it.

segments.titre: AI data centers set to double by 2030 and their power demand
segments.resume: Global data centers powering AI are on track to double between 2026 and 2030. A single facility can draw over 100 megawatts continuously, enough to drain a mid-sized town, and millions of critical systems in logistics and finance are hooked into them, all plugged into a flawed grid.
segments.texte: As AI begins to take over everyday life, the global data centers that power them are on track to double between 2026 and 2030. Just one of these facilities can easily draw upwards of 100 megawatts of continuous power, enough to drain an entire mid-sized town. Worse, millions of critical systems, from global logistics and financial systems are hooked into them. But the demands of the AI network have been plugged into a grid that is fundamentally flawed.

segments.titre: Inverter-based renewables removed the grid's mechanical inertia
segments.resume: High-voltage networks are shifting from fossil fuel and hydroelectric plants to inverter-based renewables like wind and solar. The old heavy spinning turbines acted as shock absorbers against voltage surges and frequency spikes, including from solar weather; green grids don't spin and cannot absorb a massive electrical shock, leaving the digital economy exposed.
segments.texte: In recent decades, we have reshaped the rules of electrical engineering. To combat the climate crisis, high-voltage networks are increasingly shifting away from fossil fuels and hydroelectric facilities. Instead, they’re moving toward inverter-based renewable energy, like wind and solar power. It’s a huge victory for the planet, but a massive mistake for our security. Because by abandoning the old school power plants, the main shield of the grid has been stripped away… the mechanical inertia. The old system made use of heavy, rapidly spinning mechanical turbines essentially acting like giant shock absorbers. They soaked up and smoothed out the random voltage surges or sudden spikes in frequency that can occur randomly, including solar weather phenomena. But green energy grids don’t spin. They don’t have the ability to absorb a massive electrical shock. In essence, in trying to save our planet, we’ve torn down our own defenses at the exact moment our digital economy became reliant on an uninterrupted flow of power. And that flow could be interrupted at any second.

segments.titre: The sun's first attack: the solar flare
segments.resume: A solar flare is an intense burst of electromagnetic radiation that reaches Earth in 8 minutes at the speed of light. It ionizes the upper atmosphere, knocking out aviation, maritime and emergency communications, and blinds satellites and GPS with X-rays and ultraviolet radiation. The second attack, the killer, is introduced.
segments.texte: When the sun unleashes an explosive eruption, it launches two major attacks on our planet. The first is a solar flare. An intense burst of electromagnetic radiation travels at the speed of light, slamming into the Earth in just 8 minutes. The flare ionizes Earth’s upper atmosphere, knocking aviation, maritime, and emergency communications offline. Satellites and GPS signals are blinded as the atmosphere is flooded with X-rays and extreme levels of ultraviolet radiation. But the second attack is the killer.

segments.titre: Coronal mass ejections and geomagnetic storms
segments.resume: A CME is a wave of magnetized plasma carrying billions of tons of material at up to 3,000 km/s; it takes days to arrive but is far more destructive. Compressing Earth's magnetic field, it triggers geomagnetic storms that push currents out of the ground into substations and long power lines, causing blackouts and transformer damage, while particles degrade satellites and GPS.
segments.texte: The coronal mass ejection, or CME. This is a massive wave of magnetized plasma and embedded magnetic fields blasted straight from the Sun's outer atmosphere. Packed with billions of tons of solar material, CMEs travel up to 1,900 miles per second (3,000 kilometers per second). This means it can take several days to reach the Earth’s atmosphere. That’s the good news. The bad news is they are infinitely more destructive. When a CME collides with our protective magnetic field, they can violently compress it, triggering geomagnetic storms. This forces the electrical currents straight out of the ground below our feet. Those rogue currents flood into high-voltage substations and surge along long-distance power lines, causing widespread blackouts and transformer damage. At the exact same time, high energy particles hit our satellite networks, degrading orbital tracking and killing off GPS.

segments.titre: The 1859 Carrington Event
segments.resume: In September 1859 the most intense geomagnetic storm on record, the Carrington Event, hit before the internet and AI. Telegraph systems failed across Europe and North America, operators suffered electric shocks, and telegraph pylons threw sparks that started fires.
segments.texte: Humanity got a glimpse of this power back in September 1859, during the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history: the Carrington Event. This was before the internet, AI, and green-energy power grids. But people still saw the effects. Telegraph systems across Europe and North America failed. Operators suffered electric shocks. Telegraph pylons spontaneously threw sparks out causing several fires to break out.

segments.titre: A Carrington-class storm today: $2 trillion in damage
segments.resume: Models suggest a Carrington-class storm today could cause up to $2 trillion in direct damages, roughly 15 times Hurricane Katrina's destruction in 2005. Unlike a local disaster it would act on a planetary scale, disabling energy networks across large parts of the world within seconds.
segments.texte: Experts believe that if a severe Carrington-class solar storm were to strike Earth today, the effects would be unprecedented. Some models suggest the direct damages could reach up to $2 trillion, roughly 15 times the initial destruction caused by Hurricane Katrina in 2005. And unlike a bad storm, tornado, or tsunami, a Carrington-style space event would act on a planetary scale. Energy networks across large parts of the world would be disabled in a matter of seconds. Paralyzed power lines would only be the beginning.

segments.titre: EHV transformers: the bottleneck that could take a decade to rebuild
segments.resume: Extra high voltage (EHV) transformers weigh hundreds of tons and control power flow between plants, substations and national grids. They are custom-engineered, so building one can take years; if hundreds are fried at once the supply chain collapses and rebuilding could take a decade, leaving populations and the tech economy without stable power.
segments.texte: The extra high voltage (EHV) transformers, which control the flow of power between plants, substations, and national grids would be especially vulnerable. Weighing several hundred tons each, these monstrous components form the backbone of 21st century electrical grids… and they’re not easy to make. Rather than being mass produced on assembly lines, EHV transformers are custom-engineered and highly-specialized. Even in a booming economy, it can take several years to build a single unit. If a solar storm fries hundreds of these giant transformers simultaneously across the globe, the supply chain quickly collapses. Because of this, the effects of a Carrington-scale CME wouldn’t just last for a few months, it could take a decade to rebuild our energy infrastructure. Vast swathes of the population - as well as large parts of the tech economy - would be forced to operate without a stable source of electrical power.

segments.titre: The deep core model and the blindspot in solar science
segments.resume: For over a century the global grid was designed around a scientific blindspot: astrophysicists believed the solar dynamo, the engine of the sun's magnetic field, operated only deep in the core. Under this deep core model space weather was slow and predictable and storms could be tracked days ahead; the model was incomplete.
segments.texte: So, how did it get to this? How could the world’s top engineers allow our entire civilization to be built on a knife edge? They had no idea the danger was real. For over a century, the global power grid was designed around a massive scientific blindspot. Astrophysicists believed that the solar dynamo - the “engine” of the sun’s magnetic field - only operated deep inside the solar core, tens of thousands of miles beneath the surface. Under this“deep core” model, space weather moved slowly and predictably. Scientists thought they could always stay one step ahead, tracking solar storms days and weeks in advance to protect Earth. Unfortunately, the model was wrong. Or, to be more exact, it was incomplete.

segments.titre: Kelvin-Helmholtz instability explained
segments.resume: In the 1860s Lord Kelvin and Hermann von Helmholtz described Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI): two layers of fluid or gas sliding past each other at different speeds create violent rolling disturbances, like wind over a lake. It appears in clouds and in the atmospheres of Jupiter and Saturn.
segments.texte: While everyone was busy focusing on the sun’s core, they completely missed the chaotic high-speed physics unraveling across its surface. And this was partly because they were working blind. Back in the late 1860s, two of the top physicists of the time, Lord Kelvin and Hermann von Helmholtz, came up with a concept called Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI). It happens when 2 layers of fluid or gas scrape past each other at different speeds or in different directions, creating violent rolling disturbances at the edge. It’s like when wind whips across the surface of a calm lake, causing ripples forming and waves breaking. We can observe this phenomenon in atmospheric cloud formations and even the planetary atmospheres of Jupiter and Saturn.

segments.titre: The deep core dogma persists for lack of a powerful telescope
segments.resume: About a century later solar physicists realized KHI should apply to the sun's plasma surface, but no telescope was powerful enough to prove it. The deep core model stayed absolute law, energy infrastructure decisions assumed predictable, survivable storms, and the myth only begins to crumble in 2026.
segments.texte: About a century later, solar physicists realized this same violent churning should apply to the superheated plasma ocean that covers the surface of the sun. The problem was that they didn’t have a powerful enough telescope to prove it. Without empirical evidence to rely on, the scientific community still treated the “deep core” model as absolute law. They assumed that any surface plasma dynamics were the side-effects of more powerful magnetic flows far below them. And the wider world bought into that assumption. segments.titre: MIT models: the sun's surface, not its core, drives storms
segments.resume: Researchers at MIT built precise numerical models of solar plasma flow and found that small plasma disturbances in the upper layers generate powerful magnetic field patterns. It would be the surface, not the core, causing flares and storms, but they needed detailed images of the sun's surface as proof.
segments.texte: long-standing myth is beginning to crumble. It began when researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, or MIT, developed highly precise numerical models of solar plasma flow. The team realized that small plasma disturbances in the sun’s upper layers were generating powerful magnetic field patterns. In other words, it wasn’t the core causing solar storms and flares, but the surface. The team had a theory, but they still needed proof. And the only way to get it was to capture detailed pictures of the sun’s surface, which was something that had been almost impossible.

segments.titre: Photosphere granules and the challenge of spotting KHI
segments.resume: The sun is about 93 million miles away and its photosphere is covered in granules over 1,200 miles across, made of plasma that rises, cools and sinks. KHI waves along their edges would span about 40 miles, like spotting a coin from 100 miles away, which ground-based telescopes could not do.
segments.texte: The sun is approximately 93 million miles (149.6 million km) away from us. Its visible surface - known as the photosphere - is a violent, bubbling landscape, covered in granules. A single granule can measure over 1,200 miles (1,931 km) across, and is made up of superheated plasma. This rises up from below, cools at the surface, and sinks back down at the granule’s boundaries. If the wave-like structures caused by KHI existed along those edges, they’d measure around 40 miles (64 km) from peak to peak. Trying to spot something of that size from nearly 100 million miles (161 million km) away is like asking someone to identify a single coin from a distance of 100 miles (161 km) Conventional ground-based telescopes didn’t stand a chance. So, scientists built a better one.

segments.titre: The Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope and its Fast Cam
segments.resume: Located in Hawaii at 10,000 feet and costing nearly $350 million, the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope has a 13 foot mirror and collects about 7 times more light than previous models. Online since 2021, it gives very clear images of the sun; in 2026 it was pointed at an active region to test a high speed Fast Cam.
segments.texte: Sitting 10,000 feet (3,000 meters) above sea level in Hawaii and costing nearly $350 million, it’s called the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope. Equipped with a 13 foot (3.96 meter) mirror, it’s capable of collecting around 7 times more light than any previous model. And in 2021, it came online, instantly providing some of the clearest images of the sun ever seen. In 2026, researchers pointed it towards a particularly active region of the sun’s photosphere in order to test a high speed “Fast Cam.”

segments.titre: Proof of solar KHI: 47 wave crests and plasma whirlpools
segments.resume: In minutes the telescope captured 47 curling wave crests along plasma granule edges, clear evidence of KHI on the sun. Magnetic fields act like rubber bands resisting the waves; when fast plasma overwhelms them it forms whirlpool-like vortices rising hundreds of feet, with millions forming and collapsing constantly.
segments.texte: In just a few minutes, it proved its worth and shattered a century-long myth, capturing clear images of 47 curling wave crests along the edges of plasma granules: clear evidence of Kelvin Helmholtz Instability on the solar surface. But this isn’t like wind blowing across a lake on Earth. The sun’s superheated plasma is interwoven with huge magnetic fields that act like rubber bands. They exert a continuous force that fights against the waves, trying to keep the plasma in place. For a wave to form and curl across the sun’s surface, fast-moving plasma has to move across a slower-moving stream with such force that it overwhelms the magnetic fields. The result is terrifying. Instead of ripples, magnetized plasma waves stretch upward into curling whirlpool-like vortices, rising hundreds of feet into the air. Millions of these whirlpools are constantly forming, spinning, and collapsing. And that wasn’t the only discovery.

segments.titre: First sighting of torsional Alfven waves
segments.resume: In October 2025 the telescope captured the first physical evidence of small-scale torsional Alfven waves in the sun's upper atmosphere, theorized in the 1940s by Hannes Alfven. These magnetic fluctuations carry energy along magnetic fields; they appear as high-speed magnetic corkscrews in coronal loops, previously seen only as large swaying movements.
segments.texte: In October 2025, the telescope captured the first physical evidence of another threat: small-scale torsional Alfven waves twisting across the sun’s upper atmosphere. First theorized in the 1940s by the Swedish engineer and physicist, Hannes Alfven, these waves are magnetic fluctuations that act like high voltage conduits, throwing massive amounts of energy along the sun’s magnetic fields. Before this breakthrough, scientists could only see large swaying movements across arch-like plasma structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, known as coronal loops. But it was only with the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope that they were able to isolate them and see them for what they really were: high-speed magnetic corkscrews, twisting and turning plasma back and forth at ultra-fast speeds. segments.titre: The Coronal Heating Paradox solved by flux braiding
segments.resume: The corona reaches about 2 million degrees Celsius while the photosphere stays at 5,500 degrees: the Coronal Heating Paradox. Plasma whirlpools drag magnetic fields together in flux braiding; tension builds in the knots, lines snap and reconnect, and bursts of energy heat the outer atmosphere.
segments.texte: KHI phenomena on the solar surface helped solve a mystery that had plagued scientists for decades: the Coronal Heating Paradox. The outer atmosphere of the sun - the corona - can reach up to 3.6 million degrees Fahrenheit (2 million degrees Celsius), yet the photosphere stays at a far cooler 9,900 degrees Fahrenheit (5,500 degrees Celsius). It makes no sense and has stumped scientists for years. The newly-discovered waves and whirlpools change everything. As millions of plasma whirlpools rage along granule boundaries, their movements drag magnetic fields together, a process known as “flux braiding”. It’s like twisting strands of magnetic rope into tightly contorted knots. Then, as the magnetic tension builds up inside those knots, the tangled lines snap and reconnect, releasing enormous and continuous bursts of energy that heat up the outer atmosphere.

segments.titre: Solar storms are far less predictable than believed
segments.resume: These discoveries rewrite how solar flares and CMEs are triggered: classic models assumed a gradual, predictable build-up, but violent waves across the solar surface are the real agitators. Solar storms are far less predictable, just as civilization has plugged into an unshielded grid, and the window to minimize losses is closing.
segments.texte: Unfortunately, these discoveries also revealed a frightening new threat for life on Earth. They rewrote the rules of how solar systems are triggered. Before then, classical space weather models suggested that solar flares and CMEs needed a gradual, slow, and predictable build-up. But the discovery of KHI proves that violent waves screaming across the solar surface are the real agitators. This means that solar storms are nowhere near as predictable as previously believed. The implications of this are enormous. And the timing couldn’t be worse. At the very moment that human civilization has basically plugged itself into an unshielded electrical grid, we’re realizing it could be wiped out without warning. There’s nothing we can do to stop it. And the window we have to minimize the losses is closing.

segments.titre: No warning: transformer overload and the digital blackout
segments.resume: There would be no warning time to adjust voltages and isolate vulnerable substations; a CME could arrive without alarms. Currents overload the iron cores of EHV transformers, insulating oil boils, components degrade and power stations burn. Industries would stall and countries would fight over the first replacement transformers.
segments.texte: We thought we’d have ample warning time, allowing us to adjust network voltages and isolate the most vulnerable substations. But that’s not how it works. A CME could come at almost any time. It would release huge clouds of radiated energy without sounding the alarms beforehand. When that wave collides with our atmosphere, it will kick start a catastrophic change. Currents would surge up and slam into a modern grid unable to cope with them. The iron cores of EHV transformers would become overloaded and internal operating temperatures would rise in a matter of seconds. Insulating oil would bubble and boil, structural components would degrade, and entire power stations go up into flames. We would be starting down the barrel of a digital blackout. There’s no telling how the wider world would cope with that. Industries would struggle to function without power. segments.titre: The Centennial Gleissberg Cycle: the sun leaves its quiet phase
segments.resume: The sun follows an 11-year cycle plus the Centennial Gleissberg Cycle, which rises and falls every 80 to 100 years. The sun has just finished the fall and is starting to rise: while humanity built the internet, satellites, grids and AI, the sun was in a cosmic lull, and serious space weather in recent years may be a sign.
segments.texte: more concerning is that we may be entering an era in which severe solar storms are about to become much more frequent and dangerous. The sun operates on an 11-year cycle, but historical records and recent satellite data also suggest that there are additional patterns at play. One of those patterns is known as the Centennial Gleissberg Cycle - a spinning wheel of solar storm intensity that rises and falls every 80 to 100 years. Analysis reveals that the sun has just finished the “fall” of that cycle and is about to start rising back up again. In other words, for the last few decades, while humanity was building the internet, satellites, continental power grids, and investigating artificial intelligence, our sun was going through a kind of “quiet phase” or “cosmic lull.” Now, it’s roaring back to life, which may explain why we’ve already started to see some serious space weather over the last couple of years.

segments.titre: The 2024 Gannon Storm and the expected rise in solar activity
segments.resume: The 2024 Gannon Storm involved a sunspot 17 times Earth's diameter that emitted 8 CMEs, several aimed at Earth, triggering G5 geomagnetic storm conditions and one of the largest satellite migrations in history. Some experts expect a clear spike in solar activity in the decades ahead.
segments.texte: The “Gannon Storm” of 2024 involved a highly active sunspot - 17 times the diameter of Earth - emitting no fewer than 8 CMEs, several of which were directed towards Earth, triggering G5-level - the highest level - geomagnetic storm conditions and one of the largest satellite migrations in history. Based on this evidence, some experts believe that the decades ahead of us will see a clear spike in solar activity. This will increase the odds of severe geomagnetic storms occurring across our world.

segments.titre: Fragile infrastructure, an active sun and hopes for better forecasting
segments.resume: Humanity is edging toward a cliff: fast technology, fragile infrastructure, a sun entering a more violent era. With the new data scientists might build more accurate forecasting models to pinpoint when flares and CMEs occur, but until then we must hope the next Carrington Event is still years away.
segments.texte: Humanity is edging closer to the edge of a cliff. Our technology is moving faster than ever, but the infrastructure that powers has never been so fragile. We are completely exposed just as our local star is entering a new era of heightened violent activity,. And we’ve just uncovered the truth. But perhaps, with that new data at their disposal, scientists can begin to understand the chaotic physics of the sun’s surface waves. If they move quick enough, they might be able to build stronger, more accurate forecasting models. Models that allow them to pinpoint the moments when flares and CMEs are most likely to occur. Until then, humanity will have to live in hope that the next “Carrington Event” is still several years away. It might be.

segments.resume: Closing: as the sun begins its next active chapter, the time left to insulate infrastructure is rapidly running out. Much remains unknown about our star and its surroundings, and viewers are pointed to the video "What's Directly Above And Below The Sun?".
segments.texte: But one thing’s for sure: as our star begins its next active chapter, the time we have left to insulate our infrastructure is rapidly running out. There’s still so much we don’t know about our own star, including its surroundings. And those blind spots might be deadly.
